extracted.intended_audience: employers, workplace safety professionals, labor representatives, state regulators, and public commenters on OSHA rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Federal Register notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) describing OSHA's basis for and elements of a proposed Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard for indoor and outdoor workplaces, summarizing existing federal/state/consensus guidance and enforcement practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIOSH 2016 recommended provisions for heat protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2016 NIOSH criteria document recommends various provisions to protect workers from heat stress, including rest breaks, hydration, shade, acclimatization plans, and worker training. It also recommends that no worker be “exposed to combinations of metabolic and environmental heat greater than” the recommended alert limit (RAL) for unacclimatized workers or the recommended exposure limit (REL) for acclimatized workers, and that environmental heat be assessed with measurements of WBGT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIOSH specifies both administrative and environmental controls (rest, water, shade, acclimatization, training). Environmental assessment should use WBGT; thresholds (RAL/REL) differ for unacclimatized vs. acclimatized workers. The NPRM cites the NIOSH document as a central scientific basis for exposure limits and required protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: OSHA General Duty Clause violation elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a violation of the General Duty Clause, OSHA must establish that: (1) the employer failed to keep the workplace free of a hazard to which its employees were exposed; (2) the hazard was recognized; (3) the hazard was causing or likely to cause death or serious injury; and (4) a feasible means to eliminate or materially reduce the hazard existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA must prove each element in an enforcement proceeding; reliance on expert testimony is common. The text explains limitations of the General Duty Clause (difficulty proving a recognized hazard and obtaining abatement before harm) and uses these elements to justify the need for a specific standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: WBGT-based assessment (ISO 7243 / ACGIH TLVs)
rubrics_metrics.description: ISO 7243 and ACGIH TLVs use WBGT (wet bulb globe temperature) values, along with metabolic rate (workload categories), to assess heat stress in work environments. ACGIH provides clothing adjustment factors added to measured WBGT to account for impaired thermal regulation due to clothing or PPE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WBGT must be interpreted together with metabolic rate and clothing adjustments. The NPRM cites ISO 7243 as an accepted method for assessing heat stress; clothing and PPE can meaningfully change allowable exposures by increasing apparent WBGT via adjustment factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: State heat-standard initial triggers (temperature/metric thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: State standards use various triggers to require employer protections: examples include ambient temperature triggers (California outdoor 80 °F; California proposal indoor 82 °F), heat index triggers (Oregon 80 °F heat index; Maryland proposal 80 °F heat index), and WBGT-based thresholds (Minnesota indoor: 86 °F WBGT for light work; 80 °F moderate; 77 °F heavy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States differ in both the metric used (ambient temperature, heat index, WBGT) and numeric thresholds. Minnesota uses a 2-hour time-weighted average permissible exposure limit rather than a simple trigger. High-heat triggers (e.g., 90–95 °F) are handled separately in some state rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-required baseline protections (water, shade, rest, plans, training, acclimatization, observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most State standards require employers to provide water, shade or cool-down means, rest breaks as needed, emergency response plans, acclimatization provisions, training for employees and supervisors, and a heat-illness prevention plan (often written). Many require observation/supervision and monitoring of new employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All State standards require training; except Minnesota, states listed require at least one quart of water per hour per employee, emergency response planning, acclimatization, and access to shaded break areas. California requires written plans in English and in languages understood by the majority of workers and close monitoring of new employees for the first 14 days; Washington and Oregon require training in a language workers understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: State high-heat additional protections (work-rest schedules, supervision, meetings, assessment and control)
rubrics_metrics.description: When high-heat triggers are met, State rules add protections such as specified work-rest schedules, enhanced observation/supervision, pre-shift meetings, and requirements to assess and implement control measures (measuring temperature/heat index, identifying environmental risk factors, and using specified controls).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-heat triggers vary by state (e.g., California outdoor 95 °F for some industries; Washington 90 °F; Oregon 90 °F heat index; Colorado agriculture 95 °F or other conditions). Additional high-heat provisions often focus on more frequent breaks, closer supervision, and active assessment/control of environmental risk factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: NACOSH Work Group recommended elements for a federal heat standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The NACOSH Heat Injury and Illness Prevention Work Group recommended that any proposed standard include: a written exposure control plan/heat illness prevention plan; training; environmental monitoring; workplace control measures; acclimatization; worker participation; and emergency response. NACOSH amended to ask OSHA to include a model written plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements were developed after stakeholder review and are presented as recommended required components of a federal regulatory standard to ensure comprehensive prevention and response systems, including model plan language to aid compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: OSHA inspection and enforcement triggers and emphasis programs
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's 2021 Inspection Guidance established days when the heat index exceeds 80 °F as 'heat priority days' to increase enforcement. Regional Emphasis Programs (REPs) and the National Emphasis Program (NEP) target inspections for heat-related hazards; some REPs allow inspections when the high temperature is forecast above 80 °F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM describes how OSHA uses administrative programs (REPs, NEP) and guidance to prioritize inspections during warm conditions and in specific industries. These are enforcement/prioritization rubrics rather than legally binding standards; they explain current enforcement practice and rationale for a binding standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existing OSHA standards' coverage and limitations for heat hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing standards that touch on heat issues include Recordkeeping (29 CFR 1904.7), Sanitation standards (various 29 CFR provisions requiring potable water), Safety Training and Education (29 CFR 1926.21), and PPE standards (29 CFR 1910/1915/1917/1926 provisions). These have requirements (e.g., make potable water available, record/report illnesses) but do not specify quantities, hydration encouragement, or explicitly identify hazardous heat as a covered hazard for training or PPE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes these existing standards have been insufficient to protect workers from hazardous heat because they lack specifics (e.g., no mandated water quantities, no explicit PPE/training requirements for heat), supporting the need for a dedicated standard that prescribes concrete abatement measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military and agency heat-exposure guidance and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. Armed Forces guidance includes WBGT-based requirements and exposure limits: Army TRADOC Regulation 350-29 sets rest and water consumption requirements based on WBGT and work intensity; the Navy uses Physiological Heat Exposure Limit curves and limits nonessential outdoor activity when WBGT exceeds 90 °F; tri-service and service-specific bulletins recommend acclimatization, work-rest cycles, hydration and electrolyte replacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military standards provide operational examples of WBGT-triggered work limitations, rest/water requirements, and activity cessation thresholds; OSHA cites these as additional authoritative approaches for determining practical exposure-response controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and monitoring of environmental heat (including tools and app limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Environmental heat should be assessed using WBGT measurements (per NIOSH/ISO/ACGIH). OSHA and NIOSH co-developed a Heat Safety Tool smartphone app that provides outdoor, location-specific temperature, humidity, and heat index readings; indoor measurements must be collected and manually entered for accurate calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The app and other guidance provide operational monitoring tools but are not legally enforceable. The NPRM emphasizes that accurate environmental measurement (preferably WBGT) is important for triggering protections and for implementing exposure-control plans; reliance on ambient temperature or heat index may differ across standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual definition and components of heat stress and heat strain
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat stress is a person's total heat load from (1) environmental heat (including machinery), (2) metabolic heat from exertion, and (3) heat retained due to clothing or PPE. Heat strain is the body's physiological response (e.g., increased core temperature, heart rate, sweating) that can lead to heat-related illnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective assessment and controls must consider all components (environmental, metabolic, clothing). Factors such as air flow and humidity affect cooling mechanisms (radiation, convection, evaporation, conduction) and therefore influence both monitoring choices (WBGT vs. ambient temp) and appropriate controls (rest, hydration, clothing/PPE adjustments).
